To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the emergence of equivalence classes is not a necessary condition for the development of conditional discrimination control, 2) conditional discriminations can be reversed by changing the reinforcement contingencies for comparison stimuli, 3) conditional control is disrupted by the reversal of baseline relations, and 4) the disruption of conditional control by the reversal of relations is greater in young children than adults.
the emergence of stimulus equivalence was observed in children and that the equivalence class was disrupted when the contingencies were changed in a manner that reversed the baseline relations.
the emergence of stimulus equivalence is a function of the conditional relations established in training.

the development of stimulus equivalence in children and with the effects of stimulus control reversal on established equivalence classes.
the development of equivalence relations in young children.
the development and use of behavioral procedures for the assessment of equivalence-class formation and reorganization in young children.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of the present study do not support the existence of a robust and stable equivalence relation in children.

, in the absence of a more complete understanding of the factors involved in the development of equivalence-class performance, the present study suggests that the development of equivalence relations in young children is a complex process that requires further investigation.

, while stimulus equivalence is a robust phenomenon in adults, the emergence of equivalence classes in young children appears to be more sensitive to changes in baseline conditions.
